claim: Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS) is a pleiotropic genetic disease characterized by obesity, polydactyly, renal dystrophy and cystic kidneys.
source: Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS) is a pleiotropic genetic disease (Beales et al., 1997; Zaghloul and Katsanis, 2009) characterized by obesity, polydactyly, renal dystrophy and cystic kidneys.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Beales et al., 1997; Zaghloul and Katsanis, 2009).

claim: BBS phenotypes are associated with malfunctions of cilia.
source: These phenotypes are associated with malfunctions of cilia, small antenna-like structures on almost every cell, which perform important sensory and regulatory functions.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the relationship between BBS and ciliary dysfunction.

claim: More than 19 genes have been found mutated in BBS which account for about 80% of clinically examined cases.
source: Up to now more than 19 genes have been found mutated in BBS which account for about 80% of the clinically examined cases (Khan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Khan et al., 2016.

claim: Eight BBS gene products form a stable complex called the BBSome.
source: Of these, eight BBS gene products were found to form a stable complex called the BBSome.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about BBSome composition.

claim: BBS1 has the highest mutational load, contributing to about a quarter of all BBS mutations in Europe and North America.
source: BBS1 is part of this complex, and has by far the highest mutational load, contributing to about a quarter of all BBS mutations in Europe and North America (Khan et al., 2016; Forsythe and Beales, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Khan et al., 2016 and Forsythe and Beales, 2013.

claim: The BBSome was first identified in a pulldown experiment with BBS4 as a bait.
source: The BBsome was first identified in a pulldown experiment with BBS4 as a bait (Nachury et al., 2007), which forms a stable complex with the six BBSome proteins BBS1,2,5,7,8 and 9.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nachury et al., 2007.

claim: BBS18 (BBIP10) was identified as an integral part of the BBSome complex.
source: BBS18, also known as BBIP10, was later identified as another integral part of the BBSome complex (Loktev et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Loktev et al., 2008.

claim: The formation of the BBSome complex requires the three chaperonine-like BBS proteins BBS6, 10 and 12.
source: The formation of the BBSome complex has been postulated to additionally require the three chaperonine-like BBS proteins BBS6, 10 and 12.
evidence: The claim is based on prior postulations in the literature.

claim: BBSome subunits show a domain architecture similar to proteins from vesicle-forming complexes like COPI/COPII and clathrin.
source: BBSome subunits show a domain architecture similar to proteins from vesicle-forming complexes like COPI/COPII and clathrin (Jin et al., 2010), and from the intraflagellar transport complex (IFT) (van Dam et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jin et al., 2010 and van Dam et al., 2013.

claim: The membrane association of the BBSome is regulated by the Arf-like small G protein Arl6/BBS3.
source: The membrane association of the BBSome was found to be regulated by the Arf-like small G protein Arl6/BBS3, in analogy to the Arf subfamily proteins Arf1 and Sar1 in COPI/II and clathrin coats (Cherfils, 2014; Wieland and Harter, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cherfils, 2014 and Wieland and Harter, 1999.

claim: BBS3 in the GTP-bound conformation binds to the N-terminal ß-propeller domain of BBS1.
source: BBS3 in the GTP-bound conformation binds to the N-terminal ß-propeller domain of BBS1 (Mourão et al., 2014), thereby recruiting patches of BBSome particles, as was demonstrated on synthetic liposomes (Jin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mourão et al., 2014 and Jin et al., 2010.

claim: BBS3-induced BBSome patches are planar rather than forming cage-like structures.
source: While COP complexes bud vesicles by forming cage-like structures on membranes (Lee and Goldberg, 2010), the BBS3-induced BBSome patches seem to be planar.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee and Goldberg, 2010 and inference from comparison with COP complexes.

claim: The BBSome is attached to the IFT complex and travels together with it along the ciliary axoneme.
source: The BBSome is attached to this complex, regulates assembly and stability of IFT trains, and travels together with it along the ciliary axoneme (Wei et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2014; Pan et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wei et al., 2012, Williams et al., 2014, and Pan et al., 2006.

claim: In Chlamydomonas, the BBSome is sub-stoichiometric to IFT particles and does not influence IFT function or stability.
source: While in Chlamydomonas the BBSome is sub-stoichiometric to IFT particles and does not influence IFT function or stability (Lechtreck et al., 2009), disruption of BBSome proteins in C. elegans destabilizes the entire IFT complex and affects the cohesion between IFT-A and IFT-B (Wei et al., 2012; Pan et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lechtreck et al., 2009, Wei et al., 2012, and Pan et al., 2006.

claim: A 1:1 stoichiometry of BBSome and IFT has been reported for mammalian olfactory sensory neurons.
source: A 1:1 stoichiometry of BBSome and IFT has been reported for mammalian olfactory sensory neurons (Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Williams et al., 2014.

claim: In Drosophila, the BBSome subunits BBS2 and BBS7 are completely absent.
source: In Drosophila, which has only a limited number of ciliated cells, the BBSome subunits BBS2 and BBS7 are completely absent.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Drosophila BBSome composition.

claim: Downregulation of NPHP5 specifically reduces the ciliary localization of BBS2 and BBS5, while other BBSome subunits are still targeted to cilia.
source: Downregulation of the transition zone protein NPHP5 was found to specifically reduce the ciliary localization of BBS2 and BBS5, while other BBSome subunits (BBS1,4,7,8,9 and 18) were still targeted to cilia (Barbelanne et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barbelanne et al., 2015.

claim: Some BBSome subunits are differentially localized to different compartments of photoreceptor cilia.
source: Consistently, by determining the spatial distribution of BBSome subunits in the retina it was observed that some BBSome subunits are differentially localized to different compartments of photoreceptor cilia (Wolfrum, Spitzbarth, private notification).
evidence: The claim is supported by a private communication citation.

claim: The BBSome is believed to be responsible for the selection of ciliary transmembrane proteins for IFT-mediated transport.
source: The BBSome is believed to be responsible for the selection of ciliary transmembrane proteins for IFT-mediated transport (Berbari et al., 2008b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Berbari et al., 2008b.

claim: The hypothesis that the BBSome is mainly an import adapter is questioned by studies indicating a more crucial role in ciliary export.
source: The hypothesis that the BBSome is mainly an import adapter that regulates ciliary import of cargo proteins (Berbari et al., 2008b; Jin et al., 2010; Loktev and Jackson, 2013) is questioned by studies that indicate a more crucial role in ciliary export (Domire et al., 2011; Eguether et al., 2014; Liew et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2015; Lechtreck et al., 2013; Lechtreck et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on BBSome function in import and export.

claim: Malfunction of BBSome-mediated export can be compensated by ectocytosis of membranous buds at the tips of cilia.
source: As was demonstrated recently, malfunction of BBSome-mediated export can be compensated by ectocytosis of membranous buds at the tips of cilia where GPCRs and other cargo proteins get concentrated. This can lead to a counter-intuitive net loss of proteins that no longer get exported from cilia due to defects in the BBSome (Nager et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nager et al., 2017.

claim: Short ciliary targeting sequences (CTS) have been identified as factors modulating ciliary localization.
source: Relatively short peptide sequences, so-called ciliary targeting sequences (CTS) have been identified as factors modulating ciliary localization.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about CTS sequences.

claim: No common denominator has been identified for CTS sequences.
source: However, no common denominator has been identified and a direct physical interaction between the BBsome and the CTS was only proven in a limited number of cases.
evidence: The claim is based on the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: SSTR3 interacts with the BBSome via its third intracellular loop (3ICL).
source: One of the best-studied examples of a cilium-localized receptor protein is the somastatin receptor 3 (SSTR3), which interacts with the BBSome via its third intracellular loop (3ICL) (Jin et al., 2010; Berbari et al., 2008a; Berbari et al., 2008b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jin et al., 2010, Berbari et al., 2008a, and Berbari et al., 2008b.

claim: Mutation of the SSTR3 3ICL interaction site does not prevent SSTR3 ciliary targeting.
source: Studies on chimeric receptors indicate that even though this interaction is sufficient to target non-ciliary receptors to the cilium, it´s mutation does not prevent SSTR3 ciliary targeting (Berbari et al., 2008a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Berbari et al., 2008a.

claim: SSTR3 utilizes a complex signal for ciliary localization with more than one epitope being important.
source: This indicates that SSTR3 utilizes a rather complex signal for ciliary localization, with more than one epitope being important.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mutation of one interaction site does not prevent targeting.

claim: SSTR3 localization depends on both the BBSome and the ciliary import adapter protein Tulp3.
source: It was also shown that the localization of SSTR3 does not only depend on the BBSome, but also on other factors, such as the ciliary import adapter protein Tulp3, which regulates the trafficking of many, but not all, integral membrane cargo to the cilium (Badgandi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Badgandi et al., 2017.

claim: BBS1 is particularly important for cargo recognition.
source: The BBSome subunit BBS1 emerged to be particularly important for cargo recognition, e.g. forming interactions with the C-terminal cytosolic tails of Smoothened (Smo) and Patched (Ptch1) from the hedgehog pathway (Zhang et al., 2012a; Ruat et al., 2012; Bhogaraju et al., 2013) and of the Leptin receptor (Seo et al., 2009) and Polycystin 1 (Su et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on BBS1 interactions.

claim: Additional BBSome subunits beyond BBS1 contribute to cargo binding.
source: However, additional BBSome subunits also contribute to cargo binding: For example, the C-terminal tail of Smoothened (Smo) was shown to form interactions with BBS1,4,5 and 7 (Seo et al., 2011), and a GST-tagged 3ICL of SSTR3 interacts, with varying affinities, with all BBSome subunits (Jin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Seo et al., 2011 and Jin et al., 2010.

claim: All BBSome proteins could be overexpressed in the baculovirus/insect cell system.
source: All proteins could be overexpressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), but only BBS5, BBS9 and BBS18 were found to be soluble in significant amounts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Only BBS5, BBS9 and BBS18 were found to be soluble in significant amounts when expressed individually.
source: All proteins could be overexpressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), but only BBS5, BBS9 and BBS18 were found to be soluble in significant amounts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: BBS1 was degraded to a smaller fragment representing its ß-propeller domain (residues 1–430).
source: BBS1 was degraded to a smaller fragment representing its ß-propeller domain, which could be expressed and purified (residues 1–430).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of BBS1 expression.

claim: Other BBS subunits were only soluble in minute amounts and often co-purified with chaperones like HSP 70.
source: The other BBS subunits were only soluble in minute amounts and often co-purified with chaperones like HSP 70 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The complexes of BBS9 with BBS8 and of BBS18 with BBS4 showed the strongest improvement in solubility compared to individual components.
source: Purification of several stoichiometric complexes could be achieved, from which the complexes of BBS9 with BBS8 and of BBS18 with BBS4 showed the strongest improvement in solubility compared to the individual components.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of complex solubility.

claim: BBS9 is a central organizational component of the BBSome, forming stable binary interactions with BBS1, 2, 5 and 8.
source: The co-expression tests also placed BBS9 as a central organizational component of the BBSome, forming stable binary interactions with BBS1, 2, 5 and 8 (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: BBS chaperonins BBS6 and BBS12 stabilized each other significantly when co-expressed.
source: The BBS chaperonins BBS6 and BBS12 also stabilized each other significantly when co-expressed, but coexpressing them with BBSome subunits did not improve yields and/or purity of the latter.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of co-expression effects.

claim: Coexpressing BBS6 and BBS12 with BBSome subunits did not improve yields and/or purity of the BBSome subunits.
source: The BBS chaperonins BBS6 and BBS12 also stabilized each other significantly when co-expressed, but coexpressing them with BBSome subunits did not improve yields and/or purity of the latter.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of co-expression effects.

claim: BBS9 can be divided into an N-terminal ß-propeller domain (residues 1–368) and a C-terminal part (residues 363–887).
source: BBS9 can be divided into an N-terminal ß-propeller domain (residues 1–368) and a C-terminal part containing predicted GAE, platform and alpha-helical domains (residues 363–887) (Jin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jin et al., 2010 and domain predictions.

claim: The N-terminal ß-propeller domain of BBS9 forms a complex with BBS5.
source: We could isolate complexes of BBS5 with the N-terminal ß-propeller (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and of BBS1 with the C-terminal part.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The C-terminal part of BBS9 forms a complex with BBS1.
source: We could isolate complexes of BBS5 with the N-terminal ß-propeller (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and of BBS1 with the C-terminal part.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The C-terminal part of BBS9 elutes as a dimeric species in gel filtration.
source: Consistent with the study of Knockenhauer et al. (Knockenhauer and Schwartz, 2015), we found the C-terminal part of BBS9 to elute as a dimeric species in gel filtration, while the N-terminal ß-propeller domain of BBS9 runs as a monomer (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and a citation to Knockenhauer and Schwartz, 2015.

claim: The N-terminal ß-propeller domain of BBS9 runs as a monomer in gel filtration.
source: Consistent with the study of Knockenhauer et al. (Knockenhauer and Schwartz, 2015), we found the C-terminal part of BBS9 to elute as a dimeric species in gel filtration, while the N-terminal ß-propeller domain of BBS9 runs as a monomer (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Full length BBS9 preserves dimerization at high concentrations but shifts to lower molecular weight at lower concentrations.
source: We find that full length BBS9 preserves dimerization at high concentrations, but the elution peak shifts to lower molecular weight at lower concentrations.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of BBS9 gel filtration behavior.

claim: BBS18 dramatically improved the yield of soluble complexes when introduced into complexes with BBS1,5,8 and 9.
source: The introduction of the 10 kDa protein BBS18 however dramatically improved the yield of soluble complexes, as in a complex with BBS1,5,8 and 9.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of complex solubility.

claim: BBS18 is crucial to link BBS4 to the complex containing BBS1,5,8,9.
source: We also found BBS18 to be crucial to link BBS4 to this complex, which is consistent with an interaction of BBS18 with both BBS4 and with BBS8,9.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations and inference from complex formation patterns.

claim: Coexpression of the full ensemble of eight BBSome subunits yielded only small amounts of complex with substoichiometric amounts of BBS2 and BBS7.
source: Coexpression of the full ensemble of eight BBSome subunits yielded only small amounts of complex with substoichiometric amounts of BBS2 and BBS7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: The full BBSome was difficult to purify and ran as oligomeric species on gel filtration.
source: This full BBSome was difficult to purify and ran as oligomeric species on gel filtration.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of full BBSome purification.

claim: Complexes containing BBS18 but not BBS2 and 7 had greatly improved stability and do not oligomerize.
source: Instead we found that complexes containing BBS18 but not BBS2 and 7 had a greatly improved stability and do not oligomerize.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of complex stability.

claim: The largest and most stable subcomplex is composed of BBS1, 4, 5, 8, 9 and 18.
source: The largest and most stable subcomplex is composed of BBS1, 4, 5, 8, 9 and 18.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of complex stability.

claim: The 6mer core BBSome retains most of the functionality of the full BBSome machinery known so far.
source: We consider this a BBSome core complex since it shows the most promising structural and functional properties, as it retains most of the functionality of the full BBSome machinery known so far.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations and inference from functional assays.

claim: Coexpression with BBS chaperonins BBS6, 10 and 12 did not improve sample quality of BBSome subcomplexes or the full BBSome.
source: Of note, we did not observe any additional improvement of sample quality of BBSome subcomplexes or the full BBSome upon coexpression with any or all of the BBS chaperonins BBS6, 10 and 12.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of co-expression effects.

claim: The 6mer core BBSome could be purified in milligram quantities.
source: The 6mer core BBSome could readily be purified in milligram quantities, and is soluble up to concentrations higher than 150 µM (>50 mg/ml).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of purification yields.

claim: The 6mer core BBSome is soluble up to concentrations higher than 150 µM (>50 mg/ml).
source: The 6mer core BBSome could readily be purified in milligram quantities, and is soluble up to concentrations higher than 150 µM (>50 mg/ml).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of protein solubility.

claim: The 6mer core BBSome complex was resistant to high salt washes of up to 2.5 M NaCl.
source: The complex eluted as a single entity in all subsequent purification steps (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E), and was even resistant to high salt washes of up to 2.5 M NaCl, consistent with a previous study where the native BBSome was eluted with high salt concentrations from an Arl6 affinity column (Jin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Jin et al., 2010.

claim: The 6mer core BBSome elutes in gel filtration with an apparent molecular weight of ~400 kDa.
source: The complex elutes in gel filtration with an apparent molecular weight of ~400 kDa, in acceptable agreement with the expected theoretical mass of 336.4 kDa (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D), but less consistent with it being a dimer.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: The theoretical mass of the 6mer core BBSome is 336.4 kDa.
source: The complex elutes in gel filtration with an apparent molecular weight of ~400 kDa, in acceptable agreement with the expected theoretical mass of 336.4 kDa (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D), but less consistent with it being a dimer.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from the known molecular weights of the subunits.

claim: The 6mer core BBSome has a distorted Y-shape with pseudo 3-fold symmetry.
source: The complex has a distorted Y-shape (side view) with pseudo 3-fold symmetry and a loosely packed architecture, although we cannot identify the localization of individual subunits at this resolution.
evidence: The claim is based on electron microscopy data and 3-D reconstruction.

claim: The 6mer core BBSome has a loosely packed architecture.
source: The complex has a distorted Y-shape (side view) with pseudo 3-fold symmetry and a loosely packed architecture, although we cannot identify the localization of individual subunits at this resolution.
evidence: The claim is based on electron microscopy data and 3-D reconstruction.

claim: The 3-D reconstruction of the core BBSome has a resolution of ~23 Å.
source: The final resolution of the reconstructed model was 23 Å, as estimated by Fourier shell correlation (criterion of 0.5).
evidence: The claim is based on electron microscopy data analysis.

claim: The 6mer BBSome core was captured by Arl6•GppNHp in a nucleotide-dependent manner.
source: In pulldown experiments with immobilized Arl6, the purified 6mer BBSome core was captured in a nucleotide-dependent manner: While a 7.5 fold molar excess of Arl6•GppNHp precipitated the major part of the BBSome from solution, Arl6•GDP had no detectable affinity, which supports the notion that the BBsome is the effector of Arl6 (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Arl6•GDP had no detectable affinity for the 6mer BBSome core.
source: In pulldown experiments with immobilized Arl6, the purified 6mer BBSome core was captured in a nucleotide-dependent manner: While a 7.5 fold molar excess of Arl6•GppNHp precipitated the major part of the BBSome from solution, Arl6•GDP had no detectable affinity, which supports the notion that the BBsome is the effector of Arl6 (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The core BBSome binds to a truncated Smo receptor fragment (residues R546-L665).
source: To test whether the core BBSome can recognize known BBSome cargo proteins, we generated a truncated (residues R546-L665) version of the Smo receptor, which contains a ciliary targeting motif predicted to interact with the BBSome (Zhang et al., 2012a; Seo et al., 2011; Corbit et al., 2005). In pulldown experiments as described above (Figure 3), the binding was clearly detectable, but considerably weaker than that of Arl6•GppNHp.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and citations to prior studies.

claim: The affinity of the core BBSome for fluoresceine-labeled Smo(R546-L665) is 36.1 ± 3.9 µM.
source: In fluorescence polarization experiments (see below), we determined the affinity for a fluoresceine-labeled version of this Smo fragment to be 36.1 ± 3.9 µM.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization experiments.

claim: The core BBSome has the strongest interaction with peptides from the 3ICL and the C-terminal region of SSTR3.
source: A quantification of the signal intensities from the microarray (Figure 4C) indicates that the core BBSome has the strongest interaction with peptides from the 3ICL and the C-terminal region of SSTR3, indicated in blue and green in the intensity diagram and in the context of the snake plot of SSTR3 (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: The core BBSome binds to peptides from potential BBSome cargo proteins including GPCRs.
source: We found BBSome binding motifs in most of the GPCRs tested and in Polycystin-1, Polycystin-2, the leptin receptor and Fibrocystin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Significant BBSome-GPCR binding was almost exclusively observed for peptides from the 3ICL and the C-terminus.
source: Significant BBSome-GPCR binding was almost exclusively observed for peptides from the 3ICL and the C-terminus, which are the regions previously described to interact with the BBSome and to contain ciliary targeting sequences like Ax(S/A)xQ (Berbari et al., 2008a) or (I/V)KARK (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2013) in the 3ICL or a (F/Y/W)(K/R) motif in the C-terminal part (Corbit et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior studies on CTS sequences.

claim: The interactions with Polycystin-1 correspond to a region of 44 residues that contains a tyrosine-based sorting signal YEMV.
source: The interactions with Polycystin-1 correspond to a region of 44 residues that was shown to be important for ciliary targeting and that contains a tyrosine-based sorting signal YEMV (Su et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Su et al., 2015.

claim: No interactions were observed with the VxPx ciliary targeting signals from the C-terminus of Polycystin-1 and Rhodopsin or the RVxP motif in the N-terminal domain of Polycystin-2.
source: Finally, no interactions were observed with the VxPx ciliary targeting signals from the C-terminus of Polycystin-1 and Rhodopsin or the RVxP motif in the N-terminal domain of Polycystin-2 (Geng et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Geng et al., 2006.

claim: Multiple binding epitopes with variable affinities for the BBSome were identified.
source: Sequence analysis of the binding peptides revealed no unique, single consensus motif for BBSome binding. Instead, we identified multiple binding epitopes with variable affinities for the BBSome (see below).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental data from peptide arrays and fluorescence polarization.

claim: Dissociation constants (KD) of <25 µM were determined for the majority of the tested peptides.
source: As summarized in Table 1, we determined dissociation constants (KD) of <25 µM for the majority of the tested peptides.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data summarized in Table 1.

claim: SSTR3 CT1 peptide from the C-terminus had an affinity of 22.1 ± 1.4 µM.
source: From the 15mer peptides of SSTR3 identified in the microarray screen, SSTR3 CT1 from the C-terminus had the highest affinity (22.1 ± 1.4 µM).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claim: Elongation of SSTR3 CT1 by nine residues (SSTR3 CT2) increased the affinity to 0.11 ± 0.02 µM.
source: Elongation of this peptide by nine residues (SSTR3 CT2), which includes three residues from the 7th transmembrane region and 21 residues from the C-terminus, increased the affinity to 0.11 ± 0.02 µM, the highest of all tested peptides.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claim: SSTR3 CT2 had the highest affinity of all tested peptides (0.11 ± 0.02 µM).
source: Elongation of this peptide by nine residues (SSTR3 CT2), which includes three residues from the 7th transmembrane region and 21 residues from the C-terminus, increased the affinity to 0.11 ± 0.02 µM, the highest of all tested peptides.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claim: The peptide SSTR3-3ICL from the third intracellular loop of SSTR3 had an affinity of 12.8 ± 1.0 μM.
source: The peptide SSTR3-3ICL from the third intracellular loop of SSTR3 had an affinity of 12.8 ± 1.0 μM.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claim: Smo CT1 and Smo CT4 bound with affinities of 1.8 ± 0.5 μM and 1.1 ± 0.5 μM, respectively.
source: The identified 15mer peptide Smo CT1 and a slightly elongated 19mer Smo CT4 bound with affinities of 1.8 ± 0.5 μM and 1.1 ± 0.5 μM, respectively, to core BBSome.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claim: Smo CT2, which contains one of two polybasic sequences in the C-terminal cytosolic region of Smoothened, bound only weakly with an affinity of >100 μM.
source: Smo CT2, which contains one of two polybasic sequences in the C-terminal cytosolic region of Smoothened, bound only weakly, with an affinity of >100 μM.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claim: The 37mer peptide Smo CT3 that spans both sequences of SMO CT1 and CT2 had an affinity of 1.4 ± 0.5 μM.
source: Consistently, the 37mer peptide Smo CT3 that spans both sequences of SMO CT1 and CT2 had an affinity of 1.4 ± 0.5 μM, which is similar to that of Smo CT1 alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claim: A second polybasic sequence KRLGRKKKRRKRKKE in the C-terminal region of Smoothened (Smo CT8) had an affinity of 6.8 ± 2.5 µM.
source: A second polybasic sequence KRLGRKKKRRKRKKE in the C-terminal region of Smoothened (Smo CT8) had a significant affinity of 6.8 ± 2.5 µM, although it is much lower than Smo CT4.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claim: GPR161 3ICL peptide had an affinity of 6.3 ± 1.5 µM.
source: Of these, the peptides GPR161 3ICL and NMU 3ICL1 had significant affinities of 6.3 ± 1.5 µM and 18.1 ± 1.6 µM, respectively, while the other tested peptides only presented low affinities of >50 µM.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claim: NMU 3ICL1 peptide had an affinity of 18.1 ± 1.6 µM.
source: Of these, the peptides GPR161 3ICL and NMU 3ICL1 had significant affinities of 6.3 ± 1.5 µM and 18.1 ± 1.6 µM, respectively, while the other tested peptides only presented low affinities of >50 µM.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claim: Mutations of epitopes with basic and aromatic residues reduce BBSome binding affinity significantly.
source: For both Smo and SSTR3 we can show that mutations of epitopes with basic and aromatic residues reduce BBSome binding affinity significantly, but that there is no simple universal binding motif at least for these two GPCRs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutational analysis using fluorescence polarization.

claim: For SSTR3, the affinity is derived from all three motifs (YR, FK, and FRR) and is somewhat additive.
source: In the case of SSTR3 we targeted the three epitopes YR, FK and FRR, which were mutated to alanine in various combinations. It appears that the affinity is derived from all three motifs and is somewhat additive.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutational analysis.

claim: Mutation of two residues from each SSTR3 motif changes affinity between four and fourtenfold.
source: Mutation of two residues from each motif changes affinity between four and fourtenfold, whereas combinations with four or six mutated residues reduce affinity up to ~100 fold.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutational analysis.

claim: Mutation of three arginine residues at the C-terminus of peptide SSTR3 CT2 (RRVR, residues 333–336, mutated to EEVE) reduces affinity 42 fold.
source: The binding site is even more complex, since mutation of three arginine residues at the C-terminus of peptide SSTR3 CT2, that do not strictly follow a (F/Y/W)(K/R) annotation (RRVR, residues 333–336, mutated to EEVE), also reduces affinity 42 fold.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutational analysis.

claim: Mutation of either the WRR or the WCR motif in Smo CT4 changes affinity 9 and 11 fold, respectively.
source: The mutation of either the WRR or the WCR motif changes affinity 9 and 11 fold, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutational analysis.

claim: The combined quadruple variant of Smo CT4 reduces affinity 13 fold.
source: The combined quadruple variant reduces affinity 13 fold, again demonstrating that an extended epitope is recognized by the BBsome.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutational analysis.

claim: Arl6•GppNHp does not significantly affect the binding of cargo peptides to the core BBSome.
source: We thus tested the binding of cargo in the presence of Arl6•GppNHp, but did not find significant Arl6 dependency in our fluorescence polarization assay. By titrating either the core BBSome alone or a stoichiometric mixture of the core BBSome with Arl6•GppNHp to fluorescently labeled peptides SSTR3 CT1, SSTR3 CT2 and SSTR3 3ICL, no significant difference in binding behavior was observed (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The core BBSome represents the complete set of BBSome subunits for which analogs are found in Drosophila.
source: The core BBSome as the most stable of the complexes analyzed in our studies, composed of BBS 1,4,5,8, 9 and 18, represents the complete set of BBSome subunits for which analogs are found in Drosophila (Nachury et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nachury et al., 2007 and knowledge of Drosophila BBSome composition.

claim: BBS2 and BBS7 are absent in Drosophila and might be dispensable for many aspects of BBSome function.
source: BBS2 and BBS7 are absent in Drosophila and might therefore be dispensable for many aspects of BBSome function.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that Drosophila lacks these subunits but has functional cilia.

claim: BBS2 and BBS7 are dispensable for the formation of a stable monomeric complex that interacts with cargo and Arl6.
source: It appears that they are at least dispensable for the formation of a stable monomeric complex that interacts with cargo and Arl6.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations that the core BBSome lacking BBS2 and BBS7 can bind cargo and Arl6.

claim: The observed formation of a stable core BBSome is in contrast to previous studies suggesting that BBS6, 10 and 12 are required for BBSome formation.
source: The observed formation of a stable core BBSome is in contrast to previous co-immunoprecipitation and co-migration experiments which suggested that BBS6, 10 and 12 are required for BBSome formation (Seo et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of current experimental results with prior literature.

claim: BBS7 and BBS2 reduce the solubility of the entire BBSome complex.
source: We observed that BBS7 and BBS2, which are highly insoluble proteins by themselves, also reduce the solubility of the entire BBSome complex, in the presence or absence of BBS6, 10 and 12 or any combinations thereof.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of complex solubility.

claim: The CCT/TRiC complex and the chaperonines might have a role in folding BBS7 and BBS2 before these proteins are added to the BBSome.
source: We propose that the CCT/TRiC complex and the chaperonines might have a role in folding BBS7 and BBS2 before these proteins are added to the BBSome, which might not operate in insect cells.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a possible role for chaperonines.

claim: The assembly of the BBSome might follow two parallel routes.
source: We propose that the CCT/TRiC complex and the chaperonines might have a role in folding BBS7 and BBS2 before these proteins are added to the BBSome, which might not operate in insect cells. Nevertheless, the formation of the 6mer BBSome indicates that the assembly might follow two parallel routes, one assembling the core BBSome and the second via the BBS/CCT complex to deliver BBS7 and probably also BBS2 to the complex.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a model for BBSome assembly based on experimental observations.

claim: The insect cell expression machinery is sufficient for folding and assembly of an active core BBSome.
source: In conclusion, the insect cell expression machinery seems to be sufficient for folding and assembly of an active core BBSome.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations that the core BBSome can be produced in insect cells.

claim: The N-terminal ß-propeller domain of BBS9 binds to BBS5 and the C-terminal appendage part forms a stable complex with BBS1.
source: The N-terminal ß-propeller domain (residues 1–368) of BBS9 binds to BBS5 and the C-terminal appendage part forms a stable complex with BBS1.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of domain-specific interactions.

claim: Two of the lobes of the Y-shaped structure contain BBS1 and BBS5, respectively, while the third lobe includes BBS4, 8 and 18.
source: We therefore assume that two of the lobes of the Y contain BBS1 and BBS5, respectively, while the third lobe includes the three remaining proteins BBS4, 8 and 18.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from interaction data and EM structure.

claim: BBS9 may hold the assembly together as either a monomer or a dimer.
source: BBS9 may hold the assembly together as either a monomer or a dimer.
evidence: The claim is speculative about the oligomeric state of BBS9 in the complex.

claim: The core BBSome binds to activated GTP-bound Arl6, but not to Arl6•GDP.
source: We could demonstrate that the core BBSome binds to activated GTP-bound Arl6, but not to Arl6•GDP.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from pulldown assays.

claim: The Arl6 interaction only requires the BBS1 ß-propeller.
source: While the Arl6 interaction only requires the BBS1 ß-propeller (Mourão et al., 2014), the interaction with cargo might require the complete BBS1 protein and/or additional BBSome components.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mourão et al., 2014.

claim: A small peptide fragment from the C-terminal part of SSTR3 binds to the core BBSome with ~110 nM affinity, while the affinity to BBS1 (aa1-430) is ~100 fold lower.
source: Indeed, we were able to identify a small peptide fragment from the C-terminal part of SSTR3 which binds to the core BBSome with ~110 nM affinity, while the affinity to BBS1 (aa1-430) is ~100 fold lower (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The 3ICL of SSTR3 has similar affinities to the truncated BBS1 subunit and the core BBSome.
source: In contrast, the 3ICL of SSTR3 has similar affinities to the truncated BBS1 subunit and the core BBSome.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claim: The C-terminal domain of SSTR3 requires interactions with BBS1 and other subunits of the core BBSome.
source: These findings might indicate that, while the C-terminal domain of SSTR3 requires interactions with BBS1 and other subunits of the core BBSome, the interaction with its 3ICL is mostly mediated by BBS1 alone.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential binding affinities observed.

claim: The interaction of SSTR3 with its 3ICL is mostly mediated by BBS1 alone.
source: These findings might indicate that, while the C-terminal domain of SSTR3 requires interactions with BBS1 and other subunits of the core BBSome, the interaction with its 3ICL is mostly mediated by BBS1 alone.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential binding affinities observed.

claim: A GST-tagged 3ICL of SSTR3 binds strongly to BBS1, but less prominently to BBS4,5,8 and 9.
source: The latter is consistent with the previous finding that a GST-tagged 3ICL of SSTR3 binds strongly to BBS1, but less prominently to BBS4,5,8 and 9 (Jin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jin et al., 2010.

claim: The 3ICL of SSTR3 is sufficient to target non-ciliary GPCRs to cilia.
source: It was also shown that the 3ICL is sufficient to target non-ciliary GPCRs to cilia (Berbari et al., 2008a), but that removing this loop from SSTR3 does not prevent ciliary localization.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Berbari et al., 2008a.

claim: Removing the 3ICL from SSTR3 does not prevent ciliary localization.
source: It was also shown that the 3ICL is sufficient to target non-ciliary GPCRs to cilia (Berbari et al., 2008a), but that removing this loop from SSTR3 does not prevent ciliary localization.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Berbari et al., 2008a.

claim: The microarray data suggested no significant binding of the BBSome to the 3ICL of Smoothened.
source: For Smoothened, our microarray data suggested no significant binding of the BBSome to its 3ICL, but instead to three sequences within its C-terminal region.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from peptide microarrays.

claim: Deletion of the 17 residue polybasic motif in Smoothened had minimal effect on BBS1 binding.
source: This finding is consistent with a previous study which indicated BBS1 interaction with the Smo region Q477-L665 containing all three motifs found in the microarray, but deletion of the 17 residue polybasic motif had minimal effect on BBS1 binding (Zhang et al., 2012a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2012a.

claim: Deletion of the second, 10 residue polybasic stretch from the C-terminus of Smoothened enhanced binding to BBS1.
source: In that study, a deletion of the second, 10 residue polybasic stretch from the C-terminus of Smoothened was found to enhance binding to BBS1, which indicates a possible regulatory role of this region.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Neither of the polybasic motifs in Smoothened strongly affect the ciliary localization of Smoothened.
source: It was found that neither of the polybasic motifs are strongly affecting the ciliary localization of Smoothened (Nedelcu, 2013), supporting the notion that binding to BBSome and ciliary localization are not necessarily overlapping features.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nedelcu, 2013.

claim: The BBSome may contain an extended binding site for target molecules that recognizes general features of aromatic and basic residues rather than a specific sequence.
source: Thus we would assume that the BBSome may contain an extended binding site for target molecules that recognizes general features of aromatic and basic residues rather than a specific sequence.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from mutational analysis data.

claim: Enhanced BBSome binding almost invariantly started when the peptide walk approached an arginine residue in the corresponding region.
source: By performing a single-residue walk over the GPCR sequence we can show that enhanced BBSome binding almost invariantly started when the peptide walk approached an arginine residue in the corresponding region.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations from peptide microarrays.

claim: All tested GPCRs contain an arginine residue close to the N-terminal start of the 3ICL.
source: We observed that arginine-rich motifs enhancing BBSome binding are also present in the 3ICL: All tested GPCRs contain an arginine residue close to the N-terminal start of the 3ICL, and peptides containing this arginine have a strong tendency to enhanced BBSome binding.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis and experimental observations.

claim: CTS sequences that do not contain a clustering of aromatic and basic residues don't seem to be sufficient to bind to the core BBSome.
source: In contrast, we found that CTS sequences that do not contain a clustering of aromatic and basic residues, such as the Ax(S/A)xQ motif (Bhogaraju et al., 2013) of MCHR1 and SSTR3 as well as an (I/V)KARK motif from GPCR 161 (Bhogaraju et al., 2013; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2013) don't seem to be sufficient to bind to the core BBSome: Although we found peptides that overlap with or are in close proximity to these CTS motifs, enhanced binding to the core BBSome does not require the CTS sequence being part of the peptide.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations from peptide microarrays and citations to prior studies.

claim: Multiple aromatic/basic stretches are additive in enhancing the affinity to the core BBSome.
source: We observed that multiple aromatic/basic stretches are additive in enhancing the affinity to the core BBSome, which explains why a single denominator for BBSome interactions is hard to identify.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations from mutational analysis.

claim: BBSome binding and ciliary targeting are not necessarily related in a simple fashion.
source: It should be noted that BBSome binding and ciliary targeting are not necessarily related in a simple fashion.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from observations that some CTS do not bind BBSome and vice versa.

claim: For certain proteins the BBSome has been shown to be more important for the export phase of ciliary transport rather than its import.
source: At least for certain proteins the BBSome has been shown to be more important for the export phase of ciliary transport (Lechtreck et al., 2013; Liew et al., 2014) rather than its import, indicating that different signals might exist for import, retention or export of BBSome cargo.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lechtreck et al., 2013 and Liew et al., 2014.

claim: CTS might function as ciliary retention signals, holding the cargo protein within the cilium by interactions that prevent loading or facilitate unloading of the BBSome.
source: One scenario would be the functioning of CTS as ciliary retention signals, holding the cargo protein within the cilium by interactions that prevent loading or facilitate unloading of the BBSome.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism for CTS function.

claim: The final localization of a protein is determined by the equilibrium of interactions inside and outside the cilium.
source: The final localization of a protein would thus be determined by the equilibrium of interactions inside and outside the cilium.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a model for protein localization.

claim: The Hedgehog pathway dramatically changes the localization of the Smo and Ptch receptors.
source: Such an equilibrium is dynamic and depends on the signaling properties of the compartment, which is particularly relevant for the Hedgehog pathway which dramatically changes the localization of the Smo and Ptch receptors (Pusapati and Rohatgi, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pusapati and Rohatgi, 2014.

claim: The availability of sufficient amounts of a soluble and stable core BBSome complex will allow more detailed biochemical and structural analysis.
source: The availability of sufficient amounts of a soluble and stable core BBSome complex will allow a more detailed biochemical and structural analysis of the binding of BBSome to its cargo and the relation of that binding to ciliary transport and retention.
evidence: The claim is speculative about future research possibilities.

claim: A stable heterohexameric BBSome complex was identified that binds to GPCRs.
source: A stable heterohexameric complex was identified that binds to GPCRs with interactions that only partially overlap with previously described CTS, indicating a more complex recognition than anticipated.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from the study.

claim: The interactions between the core BBSome and GPCRs only partially overlap with previously described CTS.
source: A stable heterohexameric complex was identified that binds to GPCRs with interactions that only partially overlap with previously described CTS, indicating a more complex recognition than anticipated.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from peptide microarrays and fluorescence polarization.

claim: Arl6•GTP does not affect BBSome-cargo interactions.
source: Arl6•GTP does not affect these interactions, suggesting no direct involvement in cargo loading/unloading.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from fluorescence polarization experiments.

claim: Arl6 has no direct involvement in cargo loading/unloading.
source: Arl6•GTP does not affect these interactions, suggesting no direct involvement in cargo loading/unloading.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Arl6•GTP does not affect cargo binding.
